title: In secret
hook: if you live simply or drink only water, don't announce it (Enchiridion 47)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sheep, who give wool, not grass. Your line was show the wool. What did you do today that showed it, without a word? Day three hundred eighty-two.

Day four of a new habit. No sugar, or a cold shower every morning, or a run at six. And there it is, the itch to mention it. A casual line at lunch: oh, I don't eat sugar anymore. A photo of the sunrise from mile two. Half the pleasure of a discipline, for a lot of us, is people knowing we have it. Epictetus saw this itch in his students, and in section forty-seven he names it, with a picture of a famous philosopher hugging a frozen statue. Today: in secret.
screen: `DAY FOUR OF A NEW HABIT.` → `THE ITCH TO MENTION IT.` → `IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. Once you've trained your body to live simply, Epictetus says, don't preen about it. If you drink only water, don't announce at every chance: I drink water. Second, the statue. If you want to train yourself for hardship, he says, do it for yourself, not for those outside. Don't go hugging statues. That's a jab at an old story. Diogenes the Cynic, the ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says, used to embrace statues covered in snow in winter, to toughen himself. Epictetus admired Diogenes deeply, but he knew how easily a hard practice becomes a public performance. Third, the cold water. When you're very thirsty, he says, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one. A small, private test that nobody sees. That last part, tell no one, is the whole practice. Fourth, why secrecy matters. A discipline you announce starts working for the audience. You get the reward early, in other people's admiration, and the habit quietly changes its purpose. A discipline you keep secret has only one job: to change you. A neighbor tradition says something close. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about giving to the poor in the King James words: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Two teachers, two different reasons, each in its own house, and a shared picture: some good things grow best in the dark, like roots. Yesterday was about showing the wool. Today is about the part of the work that nobody ever needs to see.
screen: `DON'T SAY: I DRINK WATER.` · `DIOGENES AND THE SNOWY STATUES.` · `SPIT OUT THE WATER. TELL NO ONE.` · `ANNOUNCED, IT WORKS FOR THE AUDIENCE.` · then, large: `IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one discipline you keep, or would like to: a walk, a fast, a kindness, a limit on your phone, a habit of prayer or quiet. Ask yourself honestly: who knows about it, and do I want them to? Now choose one small discipline to keep entirely secret today. Picture doing it, and picture not mentioning it, even when there's an opening. The bell holds the time.
In secret. Enchiridion forty-seven: train for yourself, not for those outside. Spit out the cold water, and tell no one. Today's word.
Your line: in secret. Keep one discipline secret today. Do it, and don't mention it, not even once. Day three hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism keep their personal disciplines private, so the practice serves their own growth rather than other people's admiration.
